turn_text: I grew up in a family where I was told I could be anything that I wanted to be and sadly it wasn't until I got into the military that I realized there were restrictions on me just because I was a woman and so it just really torqued me off and I decided I was going to be a fighter pilot just because they told me that I couldn't you I'm Congresswoman Martha McSally. I was the first woman to actually fly in combat in U.S. history and then later on to command a fighter squadron in combat. I remember that first trip. It was a couple hours in the middle of the night from one base to another and my subordinates I was the highest ranking person in the car and they're all wearing jeans or khakis and polo shirts and I'm sitting there in this traditional garb which is the Abaya and Abaya Headscarf. I mean think about that. I can fly a single seat attack aircraft into enemy territory but I can't drive. and I'm told to sit in the back seat of a car, and then always be accompanied by a man. I mean, women in Saudi Arabia don't have the same rights as men, so this policy was dysfunctional on so many levels. It was bad for good order and discipline, and it was really sacrificing America's values as we were serving overseas. We were the uniform to protect religious freedoms. When we raise our right hand and we take an oath as a military officer, it's to support and defend the constitution of the United States against all enemies foreign and domestic. We thought originally it was something that the Saudis were imposing. or the State Department, and in my research I discovered that it was just a not well thought out Pentagon imposed policy. A little did I know I would start an eight year journey of researching where this policy came from and shepherded some legislation that finally overturned the ridiculous policy once and for all. The whole thing was an eight year battle. I call myself a feminist Republican and I don't believe that's an oxymoron. I believe that the values that we have in the Republican Party and what we were founded on are good for men and women in our country. I've been fighting stereotypes my whole life. I don't group men and women into categories and make stereotypes about them. But we need to recognize that I think women still have untapped potential in America, that even though we've removed most of the structural barriers, we still have some cultural barriers, and those are very real to women and young girls. And if you really believe in equal opportunity, then you need to believe in that, and you need to let women and girls be whatever it is they want to be, not what you think they should be. But if you believe that you want to have the opportunity to compete and to be able to succeed and do whatever it is that you have the potential to do, where the playing field is leveled and then you have that opportunity, then that's where I would hope we could be able to attract more women and the values of feminism really to better line up with what we believe as Republicans. We should pick the best man for the job, even if she's a woman. And that's what America is all about. And I believe that's what really my view of feminism is.

explicit_propositions.text: I became the first woman to fly in combat in U.S. history.
I grew up believing I could be anything I wanted to be.
I realized there were gender-based restrictions when I joined the military.
I identify as a feminist Republican and do not see that as contradictory.
I later commanded a fighter squadron in combat.
I wore an Abaya and headscarf while traveling in Saudi Arabia.
I was required to be accompanied by a male at all times in Saudi Arabia.
I was required to sit in the back seat of a vehicle in Saudi Arabia.
The policy requiring these restrictions was imposed by the Pentagon, not Saudi Arabia or the State Department.
I spent eight years researching and advocating to overturn this policy.

assumptions.text: Leadership excellence should be based solely on merit regardless of gender.
Gender equality is consistent with core Republican values.
Cultural norms restricting women’s autonomy undermine military effectiveness and national values.
Patriotic service requires adherence to constitutional principles including individual liberty.
Women possess untapped potential that remains constrained by societal expectations rather than capability.
Structural barriers have largely been eliminated, leaving cultural ones as the main obstacle to equity.
Feminism, properly understood, supports equal opportunity without promoting division between genders.
Military professionalism demands policies grounded in reason and fairness, not arbitrary tradition.
Personal experience with injustice provides legitimate basis for public advocacy and policy change.
True patriotism involves defending democratic ideals abroad, including gender equality.
